name: sqlite3VdbeHalt
prose: Finishes execution of a VDBE program: decides commit or rollback of the transaction or statement and updates the connection counters; defined at sqlite3.c:89199-89401 (slice cut the head). It asserts the program is in the RUN state, sets p->rc to SQLITE_NOMEM_BKPT if db->mallocFailed, closes all cursors, and for a program that read or wrote the database (p->bIsReader) enters the Btrees, treats NOMEM, IOERR, INTERRUPT and FULL as special errors and rolls back everything (or marks a statement rollback for NOMEM/FULL with a statement journal) for them, checks immediate and deferred foreign-key constraints, commits through vdbeCommit when autocommit is set and this is the only writer, and otherwise chooses a statement-level release or rollback (89228-89338). It returns SQLITE_ERROR after leaving the Btrees if a foreign-key check fails for a read-only program (89292-89295) and SQLITE_BUSY after leaving the Btrees if vdbeCommit returns SQLITE_BUSY for a read-only program (89307-89309); both early returns skip the counter updates and the change of state below. If a statement transaction is requested it calls sqlite3VdbeCloseStatement and, on failure, records the code in p->rc when p->rc was OK or a constraint error and rolls back everything (89347-89359); it sets the change count when changeCntOn is set (89365-89372) and leaves the Btrees. Then (for every program that reaches this point) it decrements nVdbeActive, nVdbeWrite (if not read-only) and nVdbeRead (if a reader), sets the state to VDBE_HALT_STATE, again sets p->rc to NOMEM if db->mallocFailed, calls sqlite3ConnectionUnlocked when autocommit is set, and returns SQLITE_BUSY if p->rc is SQLITE_BUSY, otherwise SQLITE_OK (89379-89400).
note: [R:right] reviewer: claims the early SQLITE_BUSY return does not release the btrees, but the code calls sqlite3VdbeLeave(p) before returning - right (89308-89309 and 89293-89294). Read in full; vdbeCommit, sqlite3VdbeCloseStatement, sqlite3RollbackAll and the other callees not read.

name: vdbeRecordDecodeInt
prose: Decodes an integer record field of serial type serial_type from the bytes at aKey and returns it as a signed 64-bit value; defined at sqlite3.c:90560-90592 (slice cut the head). It only reads from aKey and changes nothing. Serial types 0 and 1 give the one-byte signed value (90564-90567; type 0 is accepted only because of corrupt-database tolerance, the assert at 90562 allows 1..9 except 7 unless CORRUPT_DB), 2 gives the two-byte, 3 the three-byte and 4 the four-byte big-endian signed value, 5 gives a six-byte signed value and 6 an eight-byte signed value (90568-90588). Every other serial type (including 7 and any type of 10 or more, and the constant-integer types 8 and 9) returns serial_type minus 8, so 8 gives 0 and 9 gives 1, and aKey is not read (90591).
note: [R:right] reviewer: postcondition omits case 0, which returns ONE_BYTE_INT not serial_type-8 under CORRUPT_DB - right (90564-90567, case 0 falls into case 1). Read in full.

name: sqlite3Step
prose: Runs a prepared statement until it produces a row, finishes or fails; defined at sqlite3.c:92213-92348 (slice cut the head). If the statement is not in the RUN state: when it is in the READY state it returns (via end_of_step) SQLITE_ERROR with p->rc set to SQLITE_SCHEMA if the statement has expired, with the error text transferred when the statement was prepared with SAVESQL (92222-92233); otherwise it clears the interrupt flag when no statements are active, optionally records the start time for profiling, increments the active, writer and reader counters and enters the RUN state (92240-92261). When it is in the HALT state, it calls sqlite3_reset and goes back to restart the READY case if p->rc is SQLITE_BUSY or SQLITE_LOCKED (low byte), and otherwise returns SQLITE_MISUSE_BKPT (92264-92291). It then runs sqlite3VdbeList for an EXPLAIN statement or sqlite3VdbeExec (92299-92306). A SQLITE_ROW result sets db->errCode and returns SQLITE_ROW immediately (92309-92313). Otherwise it calls the profile callback, clears pResultRow, and on SQLITE_DONE with autocommit set runs doWalCallbacks into p->rc and changes rc to SQLITE_ERROR if that is not SQLITE_OK (92320-92325); for any other non-DONE result with SAVESQL it transfers the error (92326-92331). It stores rc in db->errCode, sets p->rc to SQLITE_NOMEM_BKPT if sqlite3ApiExit reports NOMEM (and rc likewise with SAVESQL), and returns rc masked with db->errMask (92335-92347).
note: [R:right] reviewer: omits the SQLITE_ERROR return when doWalCallbacks fails after SQLITE_DONE - right (92322-92325). Read in full; sqlite3VdbeExec, sqlite3VdbeList, doWalCallbacks, sqlite3VdbeTransferError not read.

name: sqlite3_stmt_explain
prose: Changes the EXPLAIN mode of a prepared statement; defined at sqlite3.c:93464-93495 (slice cut the head). It returns SQLITE_MISUSE_BKPT for a NULL statement (93468). Otherwise it enters the connection mutex and chooses rc: SQLITE_OK if the statement is already in mode eMode (93471); SQLITE_ERROR if eMode is outside 0..2 or the statement was not prepared with SQLITE_PREPARE_SAVESQL (93473-93476); SQLITE_BUSY if the statement is not in the READY state (93477); in the remaining cases it sets v->explain to eMode, returning SQLITE_OK at once if it already has at least 10 registers and (eMode is not 2 or it already has EQP ops) (93479-93482), and otherwise reprepares with sqlite3Reprepare, whose result becomes rc, and then sets haveEqpOps to whether eMode is 2 (93483-93486). The mode is therefore changed only on the last two paths. In every case after the selection it sets nResColumn to 12-4*explain when explain is nonzero and to nResAlloc otherwise, leaves the mutex and returns rc (93488-93494).
note: [R:right] reviewer: on SQLITE_ERROR/SQLITE_BUSY paths the explain mode is not set to eMode, contradicting the postcondition - right (93473-93478 do not assign v->explain). Read in full; sqlite3Reprepare not read.

name: DbEvalNextCmd
prose: Tcl continuation used by the "db eval" command (tclsqlite3.c:1889-1948; slice cut the head): data[0] is the DbEvalContext p and data[1] the script object pScript, and result is the result of the previous script evaluation. While rc is TCL_OK or TCL_CONTINUE and dbEvalStep(p) returns TCL_OK, it copies the current row into the interpreter variables (the array pArray or the column-name variables, with NULL columns unset when SQLITE_EVAL_WITHOUTNULLS applies) and runs the script (1904-1936). When Tcl NRE is in use it instead queues itself again with Tcl_NRAddCallback and returns Tcl_NREvalObj at once (1931-1933); this early return does not release pScript or p, which stay owned by the queued callback. Otherwise, when the loop ends, either because the row source finished, dbEvalStep returned another code, or the script returned a code other than TCL_OK and TCL_CONTINUE (TCL_BREAK, TCL_ERROR or TCL_RETURN, for example), it drops the reference to pScript, calls dbEvalFinalize(p) and frees p (1939-1941). If rc is TCL_OK or TCL_BREAK it resets the interpreter result and rc becomes TCL_OK (1943-1946); any other code, including TCL_ERROR and TCL_RETURN, is returned unchanged (1947).
note: [R:right] reviewers: (1) NRE path returns early without dropping the script ref or finalizing/freeing context - right (1931-1933 return before 1939-1941, intentional because the callback reuses them); (2) prose omits TCL_RETURN from script evaluation - right (loop condition 1904 exits for TCL_RETURN and 1943 does not convert it). Read in full; dbEvalStep, dbEvalFinalize not read.

name: DbObjCmd
prose: Tcl command procedure for a database handle command "db SUBCOMMAND ...", defined at tclsqlite3.c:2003 (slice cut the head; the function ends at 3761). It uses rc, initially TCL_OK, and pDb from cd. With objc<2 it sets a usage message and returns TCL_ERROR (2047-2050); if the subcommand name in objv[1] is not found by Tcl_GetIndexFromObj it returns TCL_ERROR (2051-2053). Otherwise it switches on the subcommand and, after the switch, returns rc (3760). Within the slice: "commit_hook" returns TCL_ERROR on more than one extra argument; with no argument it appends the current script pDb->zCommit to the result; with one argument it frees the old script, stores a copy of the new script (or 0 if it is empty), and installs DbCommitHandler (also storing the interpreter) or clears the hook (2379-2408). "complete" (when SQLITE_OMIT_COMPLETE is not defined) returns TCL_ERROR unless objc is 3, and sets the result to the boolean sqlite3_complete of the SQL argument (2416-2428). "config" returns TCL_ERROR for objc>4; with no option it sets the result to a list of every option name and its current value; with an option name (an optional leading "-" is ignored) it returns TCL_ERROR for an unknown name or a bad boolean in a fourth argument, else it calls sqlite3_db_config and sets the result to the value (2436-2498). "copy" takes 5 to 7 arguments (conflict algorithm, table, file, optional separator, optional NULL text), returns TCL_ERROR for a wrong argument count, an empty separator, a conflict algorithm that is not rollback, abort, fail, ignore or replace, an unpreparable table or a table with no columns, a malloc failure, or a file that cannot be opened (2540-2625); it then reads the file line by line in one BEGIN/COMMIT, splits each line on the separator, and binds the columns (empty or NULL-text fields as NULL) (2626-2678). A line whose column count differs from the table's, or a failing insert, stops the loop with ROLLBACK and TCL_ERROR (the failing line number is appended); success sets the result to the number of lines and returns TCL_OK (2682-2697). The two malloc failures at 2594-2596 and 2621-2624: the second one returns TCL_ERROR after closing the channel but without finalizing the prepared INSERT statement.
note: [R:right] reviewer: copy's azCol malloc failure returns without finalizing pStmt, contradicting the all-paths-finalize claim - right (2620-2625; pStmt from 2607 is not finalized there). Partly read: the slice shows cases DB_COMMIT_HOOK to DB_COPY (2379-2698); the head (2003-2055) and the closing return (3760) were read, but the other subcommand cases (2056-2378 and 2699-3759) were not read and are described only generally ("switch on the subcommand").

name: main
prose: Entry point of the tcpdmatch tool (tcpdmatch.c:56-313; slice cut the head); it has no return statement and the paths read here end in exit() calls, with the error exits using code 1 (the usage function it calls is not read here). It sets hosts_access_verbose to 2, parses the options -d (use the hosts.allow and hosts.deny tables of the current directory) and -i inetcf, calls usage for any other option or when the number of remaining arguments is not 2 (90-105). It warns if REAL_DAEMON_DIR is not accessible or not a directory (110-114), splits the first operand into daemon[@server] (taking the part after the last slash if it starts with "/", with a warning) and the second into [user@]client (120-138), analyses the inetd configuration and warns when the daemon is unknown or possibly not wrapped (147-157), checks the two access table files (162-163), and builds a request with request_init and sock_methods (170-171). If the server is a hostname or an address it calls find_inet_addr and exits with 1 when that fails, evaluates each address, and exits with 1 and an error message when there is more than one address; otherwise it sets only the server name (179-218). If the client is an IPv4 dotted-quad (and, with INET6, a numeric IPv6 address) it sets the client address, calls tcpdmatch and exits with 0 (224-239). If the client is not an address and its name is not a known host name (a pattern) it sets the client name, calls tcpdmatch and exits with 0 (246-250). Otherwise it calls find_inet_addr (exit 1 on failure), evaluates each client address, warns if the reverse lookup fails, and calls tcpdmatch once per address, printing a blank line between (260-310, the INET6 variant is 262-288), frees the lookup result, and finally calls exit(0) (312).
note: [R:n/a] previously dropped only because the name was not in the slice; main exists at tcpdmatch.c:56-313, so it is fixed. The INET6 and non-INET6 compile variants (58-62, 73-79, 182-215, 262-311) are summarised together; helper functions (find_inet_addr, tcpdmatch, usage, inet_cfg) not read.

name: rfc1048_print
prose: Prints the RFC 1048 (BOOTP/DHCP) vendor-extension area; the packet name dhcp_print does not exist, the function is rfc1048_print at print-bootp.c:585-1084 and the slice (788-1042) covers only its middle. bp points at the 4-byte magic cookie, which this function itself reads and prints, and then steps over (598-599); the caller bootp_print passes bp->bp_vend, which starts with the cookie (print-bootp.c:374-376). It then loops while a byte is readable at bp: it reads the tag; a PAD tag with ndo_vflag below 3 is skipped and an END tag with ndo_vflag below 3 returns from the function (605-608); otherwise it looks up the tag name, reads the length byte (except for PAD and END) and prints the header line (609-621), checks that len bytes are available with ND_TCHECK_LEN, which jumps to the trunc label, prints "truncated" through nd_print_trunc and ends the function if they are not (634, 1082-1083). It prints the DHCP message type, the parameter-request list, and then the data according to the tag's format character: ASCII, IP addresses, longs, shorts, bytes, hex, and special tags for NetBIOS node type, option overload, client FQDN, client id, agent circuit, classless static routes, user class and SZTP redirect (673-1066); a failing print of an ASCII string, FQDN, client id, agent circuit and user class option jumps to trunc (678, 843, 867, 912, 1019). Data left over in an option is reported as trailing data and skipped (1076-1079). When the loop ends because no byte is left, the function returns (1081).
note: [R:wrong] reviewer: the annotation says bp includes the magic cookie and the function prints it, but the actual caller passes the area after the cookie and the function does not - wrong: the function reads and prints GET_BE_U_4(bp) as "Magic Cookie" and advances by 4 (598-599), and bootp_print calls it with bp->bp_vend, whose first 4 bytes are the cookie that is compared at 374-376. Partly read: head (585-680), the case-label list (673-1066) and the tail (1070-1084); the per-case bodies of 686-770 and 788-1065 were scanned by labels and goto lines only, not read line by line.

name: esp_print
prose: Prints an ESP (IPsec) packet header and, when the build has OpenSSL (HAVE_LIBCRYPTO, 767-927) and a matching security association is configured, decrypts and dissects the payload; defined at print-esp.c:731-928 (the packet name esp_decrypt_and_dissect does not exist in the file; the slice covers 767-931, the tail of esp_print). It sets the protocol name, and if fewer than a full ESP header remains before the snapshot end it prints a truncation message and returns (753-762). It prints the SPI, sequence number and length (763-765). Then, in the decryption part, it returns without further output if no SA list exists and no ESP secret is set (769-777) and, after loading the secret, if the list is still empty; for IPv6 it returns if the payload length is zero and finds the SA with a matching SPI and destination address, for IPv4 it returns if the packet is fragmented and finds the SA likewise, and for any other IP version it returns (780-816). If no SA matched it uses the default SA, and returns if there is none (821-826). It computes the IV and ciphertext positions, prints a truncation message and returns if less than the authentication length remains, returns if the SA has no cipher, and prints a truncation message and returns if the last byte is not in the snapshot (829-873). It decrypts with do_decrypt and returns if that gives NULL (876-878), pushes the plaintext buffer (on failure it frees it and calls the ndo_error handler), reads the pad length and next header, prints a truncation message and returns if the padding does not fit (899-903), pushes the snaplen, hands the payload to ip_demux_print and pops the two packet-info levels (908-926).
note: [R:n/a] previously dropped because the excerpt name was not a function name; the function is esp_print (print-esp.c:731) and exists, so it is fixed. Without HAVE_LIBCRYPTO only the header printing (753-765) is compiled. Read from 731 to 931; do_decrypt, esp_decodesecret_print and ip_demux_print not read.

name: ip6_print
prose: Prints an IPv6 packet header and its extension headers, then hands the payload to ip_demux_print; defined at print-ip6.c:224-507 (slice cut the head), returning nothing. It sets the protocol name, prints the protocol name unless -e is given (239-245). It checks that length is at least the 40-byte IPv6 header and that the version field is 6; if either fails it prints a bracketed message and goes to the invalid label, which calls nd_print_invalid (247-248, 505-506 with the macros in netdissect.h:407-413). If the payload length field is nonzero it computes the total length and, when that is larger than length, prints a "header+payload length" message with an invalid marker and continues (273-280), otherwise the total is length plus the header size (281-282). With -v it prints class, flow label, hop limit, next header and payload length (286-300), checks the header is captured (ND_TCHECK_SIZE, which goes to trunc), and pushes a snaplen of the smaller of length and the total length (308-311). It then loops over the extension headers while data remains and the advance is positive: a header longer than the remaining length goes to trunc (321-322); hop-by-hop options are rejected with an invalid marker and return when seen twice, not following the IPv6 header, or when there is neither a payload length nor a jumbo option (341-356), and a negative advance from the option handlers (hbh, destination options, fragment, mobility, routing) pops the packet info and returns; a fragment header also returns when it reaches the end of the snapshot, and a mobility header always pops and returns after printing (357-405). For any other next-header value it computes the payload length (using the jumbo length if one was found, going to trunc if inconsistent, or going to trunc if the payload length is zero and an extension header was found), calls ip_demux_print, pops the packet info and returns (418-491). When the loop ends it pops the packet info and returns (499-500). The trunc label prints a truncation message and returns (501-503).
note: [R:wrong] reviewer: length < 40 prints a truncation marker, not an invalid marker - wrong: ND_ICHECK_ZU at 247 prints a bracketed message and executes goto invalid (netdissect.h:411), whose code at 505-506 is nd_print_invalid; only ND_TCHECK_SIZE (301) and the explicit gotos use the truncation path. Slice cut the head; function read from 224 to 507 with comments stripped; hbhopt_process, dstopt_process, frag6_print, mobility_print, rt6_print and ip_demux_print not read.

name: ldp_tlv_print
prose: Prints one LDP TLV (type, length and value) from tptr, where msg_tlen is the number of bytes left in the message; defined at print-ldp.c:238-547 (slice cut the head). It returns 0 after printing "TLV contents go past end of message" when the TLV length plus 4 exceeds msg_tlen (258-261). It prints the TLV type, length and its unknown-forward flags, advances past the 4-byte header and switches on the type (266-277). For the types it knows (common hello, IPv4 and IPv6 transport address, configuration sequence number, address list, common session, FEC with its wildcard, prefix, host address and Martini VC cases, generic label, status, FT session, MTU) it first requires a minimum remaining length with the TLV_TCHECK macro: if the remaining TLV length is smaller, that macro prints a bracketed message and an invalid marker and jumps to the invalid label, which returns tlv_len+4 (231-236, 545-546). A failed prefix decode with code -2 jumps to the trunc label, which calls nd_trunc_longjmp and does not return to the caller (364, 374, 542-543). A Martini VC FEC with VC-info-length below 4 prints a note and returns tlv_len+4 directly (416-419). The other listed types (hop count, path vector, ATM and FR labels, extended status, returned PDU or message, session parameters, label request message id) and unknown types only hexdump the value when ndo_vflag is at most 1 (524-538). In the normal case the function returns tlv_len+4 (540).
note: [R:wrong] reviewer: the truncation path uses goto trunc and likely returns 0, not nd_trunc_longjmp; GET_* macros do not check capture - wrong for the trunc label: 542-543 is exactly "trunc: nd_trunc_longjmp(ndo);" (no return 0); the only return 0 is the past-end-of-message check at 260. Read in full (comments stripped); the LDP lookup tables and decode_prefix4/6 not read.

name: lisp_print
prose: Prints a LISP control packet (Map-Register or Map-Notify); the packet name lisp_map_register_print does not exist, the function is lisp_print at print-lisp.c:227-390 and the slice cut its head. It sets the protocol name, requires MAP_REGISTER_HDR_LEN bytes to be captured (ND_TCHECK_LEN, which goes to the trunc label), prints the type through lisp_hdr_flag, and returns without printing more when the type is neither Map-Register nor Map-Notify (248-257). It then computes whether xTR data is present, reads the authentication data length and the record count (260-266). With -v it prints the record count, the authentication type looked up from the key-id field (not the key id itself) and the authentication data as hex; without -v it prints only the record count (268-277). If the record count is 0 it goes to the invalid label, which calls nd_print_invalid (280-281, 388-389). For each EID record while bytes remain (284-364) it requires the fixed record bytes to be captured, prints TTL, action and map version in verbose mode, prints the EID address for IPv4 or IPv6 and returns silently for any other address family (304-323); it then prints each locator (address for IPv4/IPv6, nothing for other families, priorities and flags in verbose mode, 327-363). After the records it prints the xTR-ID and site ID when the xTR bit is set, going to invalid if fewer than 24 bytes are available (371-376); otherwise it hex-prints any remaining bytes as data (379-382). It returns at 384; trunc prints a truncation message and returns (385-387).
note: [R:right] reviewer: prose implies auth data always; code prints it only in verbose, and prints the auth type not the key id - right (268-274; the else branch at 275 prints only the record count). Slice cut the head; function read from 248 to 390 with comments stripped; lisp_hdr_flag and the other helpers (shown, 392-450) read only briefly.

name: llc_print
prose: Prints an IEEE 802.2 LLC header and dispatches on the SAPs; defined at print-llc.c:148-403 (slice cut the head). The return value is a header length: positive when the payload was printed by a dissector or the LLC frame was fully described, negative or zero otherwise. It requires 3 captured and 3 total bytes, and prints a truncation marker plus the default hex print and returns caplen or length respectively if either is below 3 (157-166). The control field is one byte for unnumbered frames (hdrlen 3), where the check is for 3 bytes; for every other frame the control field is two bytes (hdrlen 4) and fewer than 4 captured or total bytes give the same truncation return (178-206). A frame with both SAPs global is passed to ipx_print and returns 0 (208-228). With -e it prints the LLC header fields (234-248). It then advances past the header and tries the dissectors: SNAP via snap_print returns hdrlen+5 when snap_print reports the payload printed and -(hdrlen+5) when not (257-273); STP, IP, IPX, NetBEUI and ISO CLNS with their SAP pairs print the payload and return hdrlen (275-328). Otherwise it prints the SAP names (without -e) and describes the frame: for an unnumbered frame it prints the command and flags and, for XID, handles an empty or truncated XID body with an early return of hdrlen (353-385); a supervisory frame returns hdrlen with no payload (387-393); an information frame, or an unnumbered frame that did not return earlier, ends with return -hdrlen (402).
note: [R:wrong] reviewer: says the non-U-format truncation threshold is 4 bytes while the code uses hdrlen 3 for non-U frames - wrong: the code uses hdrlen 3 only for U-format frames (182-183) and for every other frame sets hdrlen to 4 (205) and tests caplen<4 and length<4 (189-198). Slice cut the head; function read in full with comments stripped; the called dissectors not read.

name: snap_print
prose: Prints a SNAP header (OUI plus protocol id) and dispatches to the protocol dissector; defined at print-llc.c:420-608 (slice cut the head). It returns 1 after printing a truncation marker when fewer than 5 bytes are captured or present (ND_TCHECK_5 and the length check, 430-432, 605-607). It reads the 3-byte OUI and 2-byte protocol id, prints them with -e, and skips the 5 bytes (433-451). By OUI: encapsulated Ethernet and Cisco-90 call ethertype_print and return its result if nonzero (454-465); AppleTalk with ethertype ATALK does the same (467-481); Cisco CDP, DTP, UDLD, VTP, PVST and VLAN-bridge protocol ids call the matching printer and return 1 (483-503); for RFC 2684 the Ethernet, 802.5, FDDI and BPDU protocol ids skip the bridge padding (and one more byte for FDDI), call ether_print, token_print, fddi_print or stp_print and return 1 (506-573); the padding checks ND_TCHECK_LEN(p, bridge_pad) at 518, 539 and 560 jump to trunc, which prints a truncation message and returns 1 when the padding bytes are not captured. If nothing matched it prints an addresses and SNAP summary line (without -e) and returns 0 (576-603).
note: [R:right] reviewer: omits the trunc return when RFC 2684 padding bytes are not captured (ND_TCHECK_LEN on bridge_pad) - right (518, 539, 560 go to 605-607 which return 1). Slice cut the head; function read in full with comments stripped; the called printers not read.

name: lspping_print
prose: Prints an MPLS LSP-Ping packet (common header, then its TLVs); defined at print-lspping.c:488-1074 (slice cut the head), returning nothing. It jumps to the tooshort label (prints "packet is too short") if fewer bytes than the common header are present (528-529, 1072-1073), requires the header to be captured (ND_TCHECK_SIZE goes to trunc), and returns after printing a message if the version is not LSPPING_VERSION (535-539). Without -v it prints a one-line summary and returns (542-548). Otherwise it prints version, message type, reply mode, return code (with the subcode for return codes 3, 4, 8, 10, 11 and 12), sender handle, sequence number and the sent and received timestamps (553-597). It then loops over the TLVs while bytes remain: a remaining length below the TLV header size, or a TLV whose length plus header exceeds the remaining length, goes to tooshort (606-607, 631-632); a TLV of length 0 is skipped (621-625); the value must be captured (ND_TCHECK_LEN at 634). The Target FEC Stack TLV is parsed sub-TLV by sub-TLV: too little data for a sub-TLV header or its length sets tlv_hexdump and goes to tlv_tooshort (641-657); a sub-TLV of unexpected length for its type, and unknown sub-TLV types, are printed as hex through subtlv_hexdump (676, 690, 704, ..., 855); after the sub-TLV a too-short padded length prints "TLV is too short" and returns (865-871). The downstream-mapping TLV and the other TLV types are handled in the code after 878 (too-short TLV values set tlv_hexdump and go to tlv_tooshort, 880-882 and later); unknown TLV types are hex-dumped when -v is at most 1 (1044-1051). At tlv_tooshort it hex-dumps the value when -vv or tlv_hexdump applies, pads the length to a multiple of 4, goes to tooshort if the padded TLV exceeds what is left, and advances (1054-1069). It returns at 1071.
note: [R:right] reviewer: a TLV length overrun goes to tooshort, not "TLV is too short"/tlv_hexdump, and an invalid sub-TLV length sets subtlv_hexdump - right (631-632 goto tooshort; 674-677 and the matching lines for the other sub-TLV types set subtlv_hexdump). Partly read: header and TLV loop (525-660), the sub-TLV code through 862, the tail (845-882, 1036-1074); the downstream-mapping TLV and the other TLV bodies (883-1035) were scanned only for gotos (883, 911, 931, 951, 971, 996, 1017, 1030 all go to tlv_tooshort).

name: rsvp_obj_print
prose: Prints a sequence of RSVP objects from tptr (tlen bytes) for a message with the given common header; defined at print-rsvp.c:675-1915 (slice cut the head). It returns 0 at 1902 after the loop, or -1 on any error. While at least an object header remains it requires the header to be captured (ND_TCHECK_LEN, which goes to trunc), and returns -1 after printing an error when the object length is not a multiple of 4, is smaller than the header, or exceeds the remaining length (699-739). It prints the object class and class type, then switches on the class number and for known classes parses the value (session, confirm, notify request, labels, style, templates, label request, ERO/RRO, XRO, hello, restart capability, capability, session attribute, generalized UNI, RSVP hop, time values, TSPEC/ADSPEC/FLOWSPEC, filter spec, fast reroute, detour, class type, error spec, properties, message ids, integrity, admin status, label set and others, 749-1878); the many goto obj_tooshort exits (for example 753, 767, 1160) print "object is too short" and return -1 (1906-1908), goto subobj_tooshort prints "sub-object is too short" and returns -1 (1310, 1316, 1338, 1903-1905), goto invalid calls nd_print_invalid and returns -1 (1112, 1119, 1132, 1261, 1301, 1909-1911), trunc calls nd_print_trunc and returns -1 (1912-1914), and a property TLV shorter than 2 returns -1 at 1717. In the ERO/RRO IPv4 loop a sub-object whose length exceeds the remaining object length prints an error and only breaks out of that loop, and a zero length does the same (1096-1104); neither returns -1. Unknown classes are hex-dumped when -v is at most 1 (1889-1892). After each object the value is hex-dumped when -vv or the hexdump flag applies (1895-1897) and tptr and tlen advance by the object length (1899-1900).
note: [R:right] reviewer: ERO sub-object length greater than the object length prints an error and breaks, it does not return -1 - right (1096-1099, in the inner while loop at 1085). Partly read: head (675-745), ERO/RRO start (1081-1108), generalized UNI (1239-1344), properties (1705-1722) and tail (1872-1915); the bodies of the other object classes were scanned only for return/goto lines (goto obj_tooshort, invalid and trunc), not read.

name: sliplink_print
prose: Prints the direction and link-level type of a SLIP packet; defined at print-sl.c:108-168. It reads the direction byte at p+SLX_DIR and prints "I " for incoming, "O " for outgoing, or "Invalid direction %d " and sets dir to -1 (116-131). It then switches on the high nibble of the byte at p+SLX_CHDR. TYPE_IP prints "ip <length+SLIP_HDRLEN>: " (134-136). TYPE_UNCOMPRESSED_TCP reads the connection id from the ip_p field of the copy at p+SLX_CHDR into the global lastconn, prints "utcp <id>: ", and returns if dir is -1; otherwise it requires the ip header and the TCP header to be captured (ND_TCHECK_SIZE, 150-152), and stores the data length (length minus the header words) in the global lastlen[dir][lastconn] (144-154). Any other type returns if dir is -1; else if TYPE_COMPRESSED_TCP is set it calls compressed_sl_print (which itself reads the compressed header and the ip and TCP headers and updates lastconn and lastlen) and prints ": ", and otherwise it prints "slip-%u!: " with the byte value (157-166). It returns nothing.
note: [R:right] reviewer: the precondition omits that the compressed TCP path also reads the ip and TCP headers and p+SLX_CHDR+ip_p - right for the compressed path (compressed_sl_print at 251-255 checks and reads ip and the TCP header) and for the uncompressed path (144, 150-153). Function read in full (108-168); compressed_sl_print also read (203-257).

name: slow_oam_print
prose: Prints an IEEE 802.3 Slow Protocols OAM PDU; defined at print-slow.c:478-735 (slice cut the head), returning nothing. It jumps to tooshort (prints a "too short" message, 733-735) if fewer than the 3-byte common header (flags and code) remain (511-512), requires it to be captured (ND_TCHECK_SIZE), advances past it and prints the flags and code (513-522). Then it switches on the code. Information PDUs (code INFO) and event notification PDUs loop over TLVs: a TLV header that does not fit goes to tooshort (528-529, 625-626); an end-of-TLV type prints a marker and returns (538-544, 635-641); a TLV length below the header size prints a message and returns (547-551, 644-648); a TLV longer than the remaining bytes goes to tooshort and the TLV bytes are captured-checked with ND_TCHECK_LEN (553-555, 650-652). For local and remote information TLVs and the four link-event TLV types it compares the length field stored inside the TLV (info_length or event_length) with the size of the structure, hex-dumps the TLV on mismatch (563-568, 662-667) and otherwise reads and prints the structure fields; this check uses the stored field and not the TLV length, so the TLV length is not itself checked against the structure size. Organization-specific and unknown TLVs are hex-dumped (593-599, 683-689), and -vv hex-dumps every TLV (604-607, 694-697). Event notifications first skip a 2-byte sequence number after requiring 2 bytes (616-620). Loopback control requires the structure to fit (else tooshort), prints the command and skips one byte (704-716). Variable request, response, private and unknown codes are hex-dumped when -v is at most 1 (722-729). It returns at 731.
note: [R:right] reviewer: claims every read guarded, but the info/link-event fields are read without ensuring the TLV length covers the structure - right: the guard at 563 and 662 compares the structure's own info_length/event_length field, while the captured length check at 555 and 652 is against the TLV length field only. Slice cut the head; read in full with comments stripped except the field-printing bodies, which were not read.

name: tcp_print
prose: Prints a TCP header, its options, and hands the payload to a port-specific printer; defined at print-tcp.c:160-854 (slice cut the head), returning nothing. It sets the protocol name and, if the destination port field is not captured, prints a truncated source/destination summary with nd_print_trunc and returns (177-196). It prints the ports (with addresses for IPv4/IPv6), requires the fixed header to be captured (ND_TCHECK_SIZE, which goes to trunc), and returns after a message if the header length (data offset times 4) is below the fixed header size (226-234). With -q it prints the length and returns early (241-247). Otherwise it prints flags, sequence and acknowledgement (with relative values), window and urgent pointer, and, when the header is longer than the fixed one, walks the options while bytes remain (456-709): the length byte of a non-zero-length option must be at least 2 and not exceed the remaining header bytes, otherwise it goes to bad (474-475); MSS, window scale, SACK, timestamp, signature, SCPS, TCP-AO, UTO, MPTCP, Fast Open and experimental options are decoded, with LENCHECK jumping to bad when an option claims more than the header holds (482); a SACK length that is not a multiple of 8 and the invalid signature or TCP-AO cases are reported inside the option text and the walk continues (503-505, 562, 592-593); an option whose observed length differs from the stated one prints "[len N]" (700-705) and the walk ends after an EOL option (707-708). After the options it prints the length, returns if the segment has no payload (718-719), checks that the whole header is captured (nd_trunc_longjmp if not, 729-733), skips the header, handles RST segments through print_tcp_rst_data or a captured-length check and returns (735-741), and, for a forced packet type, calls zmtp1/resp/domain printers and returns (743-756). Otherwise it dispatches on the source or destination port to the application printers (FTP, SSH, telnet, SMTP, whois, DNS, HTTP, NetBIOS, BGP, RPKI-RTR, SMB, RTSP, MSDP, LDP, RESP, BEEP, OpenFlow) or, for NFS ports with at least 4 captured bytes, to the RPC printers (759-843), and returns at 844. The bad label prints "[bad opt]" and returns (845-849) and the trunc label prints a truncation message (850-853).
note: [R:right] reviewer: TCPAO invalid length prints invalid and continues; the annotation says an invalid option length returns without payload - right (592-593, 609 and then the loop advance at 697-698 continue after printing the invalid marker; only the generic option length check at 474-475 goes to bad). Partly read: head (168-250), option walk (455-530 and 585-612, 696-720), payload dispatch and tail (722-854); the individual option cases between 530 and 584 and 613-696 and the port dispatch bodies (759-843) were scanned only by their labels and gotos.

name: vsock_if_print
prose: Link-layer printer for Linux vsockmon captures: it sets the protocol name to "vsock" (251) and, when the captured length h->caplen is smaller than the vsockmon header, prints a truncation marker, adds the caplen to ndo->ndo_ll_hdr_len and returns (253-257). Otherwise it adds the header size to ndo->ndo_ll_hdr_len and calls vsock_hdr_print(ndo, cp, caplen) (258-259). It returns nothing. The packet name af_vsockmon_print does not exist in print-vsock.c; the slice (253-260) is the tail of vsock_if_print, which starts at print-vsock.c:245-246.
note: [R:n/a] still-rejected for "name not in slice"; the real function is vsock_if_print (print-vsock.c:245-260), fixed under that name. Read in full; vsock_hdr_print (a different function, 200-243) was read only enough to see it is a separate function.

name: open_interface
prose: Opens a pcap capture handle for device and returns it, or NULL when the device does not exist; defined at tcpdump.c:1294-1517 (slice cut the head); the behaviour depends on compile-time options. With HAVE_PCAP_OPEN, a device name starting with an rpcap URL prefix is opened with pcap_open: on failure it returns NULL if the error text contains "No such device" or "The system cannot find the device specified", and calls error() (which does not return) for any other failure; on success it warns if ebuf is non-empty and returns the handle (1306-1331). With HAVE_PCAP_CREATE, other devices go through pcap_create and a sequence of setting calls (timestamp precision, immediate mode, snaplen, promiscuous mode, monitor mode, timeout, buffer size, timestamp type), each of which calls error() on failure; pcap_create failing returns NULL only if the error text contains "No such device" (the Windows text is not tested on this path, 1343-1344) and otherwise calls error() (1335-1410). Then pcap_activate: a negative status closes the handle and returns NULL, after calling error() for most error codes (PCAP_ERROR, permission denied with a message, capture-not-supported with a message, rfmon-not-supported on a wlan device, and any other status), except that PCAP_ERROR_NO_SUCH_DEVICE copies a message into ebuf and does not call error() (1417-1467); a positive status prints a warning only (1468-1483). It then sets the direction if requested (error() on failure, 1485-1490). Without HAVE_PCAP_CREATE it defaults the snaplen to MAXIMUM_SNAPLEN if 0 and uses pcap_open_live, returning NULL for "No such device" and calling error() for other failures (1492-1511). In the pcap_create and pcap_open_live paths a non-empty ebuf after success produces a warning only for the open_live path (1512-1513), and the common return pc is at 1516.
note: [R:right] reviewer: claims NULL for 'The system cannot find the device specified', but the code only checks 'No such device' - right for the pcap_create and pcap_open_live paths (1343, 1508); the Windows message is tested only on the rpcap path (1323-1325), so a general statement is wrong. Slice cut the head; function read in full with comments stripped, error() and the pcap library calls not read.

name: e_inc_search
prose: Incremental history search in tcsh's line editor (ed.chared.c:1058-1259): dir is the initial search direction, F_UP_SEARCH_HIST or its forward counterpart. It returns CC_ERROR at once if the edit buffer has too little room for the prompt (1074-1075). It then loops (1077-1257). Each pass, if the pattern buffer is empty, sets the static pchar to ':' and appends '*' to the pattern (1079-1082); this resets pchar before any search has been done. It appends a prompt line ("bck" or "fwd", pchar, and the pattern) to the input buffer, refreshes the display, and reads a character; if reading fails it returns e_send_eof(0) (1101-1102). The character is handled: inserting characters append to the pattern (beep if there is no room); the incremental forward and back commands change newdir and set redo; the delete-previous command ends the search with done set when the pattern is longer than 1, else beeps; control-G sets CC_ERROR and done; control-W appends the next word at the cursor to the pattern; any other key is pushed back as a macro and ends the search with CC_REFRESH (1104-1177). It then removes the prompt line (1179-1181). If the search is not done, and the pattern has more than one character with no unmatched '[', it searches (moving the cursor on a repeated search, appending '*', calling c_search_line and, if that fails, the up or down history search), then restores the pattern length; on failure it beeps, restores the old history line and cursor, and sets pchar to '?', otherwise pchar is ':' (1183-1230); a failure to restore the history line returns CC_ERROR (1220-1224). It then calls itself recursively with newdir, and turns CC_ERROR into CC_NORM when pchar is '?' and the outer pchar was ':' (1232-1237). If the result is CC_NORM, or CC_ERROR with an initially empty pattern, it restores pchar, the pattern length, the history number (returning CC_ERROR if GetHistLine fails) and the cursor, and refreshes after an error (1241-1253). It returns ret if done is set or ret is not CC_NORM; otherwise the loop continues (1254-1255).
note: [R:right] reviewer: pchar is set to ':' on the first round even when no search is performed, so it is not unchanged - right (1079-1081 run each pass with an empty pattern, before any search; pchar is restored only later at 1243). Slice cut the head; function read in full with comments stripped; the called helpers (GetHistLine, c_search_line, e_send_eof) not read.

name: MakeLiteral
prose: Finds or adds a literal string in tcsh's global literal buffer litptr (ed.refresh.c:109-156) and returns its index with the LITERAL bit set, or '?' on failure. The text is addlit's text followed by str[0..len): when addlit is nonzero and has the LITERAL bit set, addlit's text is the NUL-terminated string at litptr+(addlit&~LITERAL)*LIT_FACTOR, when it has no LITERAL bit it is the single character addlit, and when addlit is 0 only str is used (113-125). It scans the entries (spaced LIT_FACTOR characters apart) for one with the same text followed by a NUL and returns (i/LIT_FACTOR)|LITERAL for the first match without changing the buffer (121-123, 126-128). If there is none and the buffer lacks room it grows litptr with xrealloc by 256 characters, doubled until the new text fits, updates litalloc, and re-points addlitptr when it pointed into the old buffer; a NULL result from xrealloc returns '?' (130-141). It also returns '?' when the new index litlen/LIT_FACTOR is not below LITERAL or equals CHAR_DBWIDTH (143-145). Otherwise it appends the addlit text, the str text and NUL characters until litlen is a multiple of LIT_FACTOR (at least one NUL), and returns the new index with the LITERAL bit (146-155).
note: [R:n/a] fixed-unreviewed in the packet; checked against ed.refresh.c:109-156 (the slice cut the head; function read in full). The old prose's preconditions are consistent with the code; Strncmp, Strlen and xrealloc not read.

name: pgetty
prose: Called in a child after fork to set up its process group and, optionally, the controlling terminal; defined at sh.proc.c:1992-2057, and its body exists only when BSDJOBS is defined (1994-2056), otherwise it does nothing. With POSIXJOBS and wanttty>0 it blocks SIGTSTP and SIGTTIN, saving the old mask in oset and registering a cleanup (2007-2013). Without POSIXJOBS and wanttty>0 it calls setttypgrp(pgrp) first (2016-2019). If wanttty is not negative it calls setpgid(0, pgrp); if that fails and POSIXJOBS is defined it retries with the child's own pid as group, and if that also fails (or without POSIXJOBS) it prints a "setpgid child" system error and calls xexit(0); if the retry works it sets wanttty to the new group id, so wanttty then counts as positive (2027-2041). With POSIXJOBS and wanttty>0 (including that case) it gives the terminal to pgrp with setttypgrp and runs cleanup_until(&oset), which restores the signal mask (2044-2048). In the case that wanttty was 0 on entry and the first setpgid failed, the signals were not blocked at the start (2007 requires wanttty>0) but this cleanup is still run on oset, which was never set on that path. Finally, if the global tpgrp is positive it sets it to 0 (2054-2055). It returns nothing.
note: [R:right] reviewer: wanttty==0 with a failed first setpgid sets wanttty positive but never blocked SIGTSTP/SIGTTIN or restored the mask in a matching way - right (2007 blocks only for wanttty>0; 2037 raises wanttty; 2045-2047 then runs setttypgrp and cleanup_until(&oset) on an unset oset). Slice cut the head; function read in full; setttypgrp, cleanup_until and xexit not read.

name: auto_lock
prose: tcsh's terminal lock for the auto-lock timeout (tc.func.c:691-795); returns nothing. Unless NO_CRYPT is defined it looks up the effective user's stored password hash, from getauthuid, from getspnam (retrying while errno is EINTR) or from pw_passwd, depending on the platform, and if none is found it calls auto_logout() and returns (693-748). Otherwise it cancels the alarm, prints a newline and, up to 5 times, prompts "Password:" with xgetpass and compares the encrypted answer (through the platform's crypt wrapper) with the stored hash (the AFS build also accepts a Kerberos-style AFS authentication, whose user name comes from the shell variable afsuser, else the AFSUSER environment variable, else pw_name, 752-779). On a match it zeroes the typed password, redraws the input line if GettingInput is set and just_signaled is not, clears just_signaled and returns (781-789); on a mismatch it prints "Incorrect passwd for <user>" (791). After 5 failures, or with NO_CRYPT defined, it calls auto_logout() at the end (794).
note: [R:right] reviewer: the AFS username may come from $afsuser or pw_name, not only the environment - right (759-763). Slice cut the head; function read in full; auto_logout, xgetpass and the platform crypt wrappers not read.

name: xwcwidth
prose: Returns the display width of a Unicode code point as an int; defined at tc.nls.c:38-52. If wchar is at most 0xffff it returns wcwidth((wchar_t)wchar), the library's width for that character (42-43). Otherwise it subtracts 0x10000, builds a UTF-16 surrogate pair (high 0xd800 | (v>>10), low 0xdc00 | (v&0x3ff)) in a two-element local array and returns wcswidth(ws, 2) (48-51). It writes no state of its own, and the results depend on the C library's wcwidth and wcswidth and the current locale; for inputs above 0x10ffff the pair formed is not a valid surrogate pair.
note: [R:right] reviewer: the formal contract only bounds the result and omits the exact wcwidth/wcswidth equality - right; the contract field is left empty because the result depends on the locale-dependent library functions (global state). Function read in full.

name: STRBUF##_alloc(void)
prose: Generated functions strbuf_alloc(void) and Strbuf_alloc(void) (from DO_STRBUF(strbuf, char, strlen) and DO_STRBUF(Strbuf, Char, Strlen), tc.str.c:628, 709-710). Each returns xcalloc(1, sizeof(struct strbuf)) (or struct Strbuf) (630-634), so the fields come back zeroed (len 0, size 0, s NULL) as long as xcalloc zero-fills as calloc does; the possibility of a NULL return depends on xcalloc, which was not read. The caller owns the result and releases its buffer with the _cleanup function or the whole object with the _free function.
note: [R:n/a] fixed-unreviewed in the packet; checked against tc.str.c:630-634. The claim that xcalloc never returns NULL was not checked (xcalloc not read), so the prose now says it depends on xcalloc.

name: STRBUF##_store1(struct STRBUF *buf, CHAR c)
prose: Generated static functions strbuf_store1 and Strbuf_store1 (tc.str.c:636-648). If buf->size equals buf->len it first grows buf->s with xrealloc, to 64 entries if size was 0 and otherwise to double the size, and stores the new size (639-645). It then asserts that buf->s is non-NULL (646, assert only) and writes c at buf->s[buf->len] (647); buf->len is not changed. When size differs from len, buf->s must already be a valid buffer of at least len+1 entries; this function does not check that.
note: [R:n/a] fixed-unreviewed in the packet; checked against tc.str.c:636-648 (the earlier text is consistent with the code; the extra statement about len+1 entries follows from size being at least len+1 when it differs from len and the struct being well formed, which is an assumption about callers).

name: STRBUF##_terminate(struct STRBUF *buf)
prose: Generated functions strbuf_terminate and Strbuf_terminate (tc.str.c:651-655): they call STRBUF##_store1(buf, '\0'), which grows the buffer if size equals len and writes a NUL at buf->s[buf->len]; buf->len is not changed, so the NUL is not counted.
note: [R:n/a] fixed-unreviewed in the packet; checked against tc.str.c:651-655 (and the store1 text at 636-648).

name: STRBUF##_appendn(struct STRBUF *buf, const CHAR *s, size_t len)
prose: Generated functions strbuf_appendn and Strbuf_appendn (tc.str.c:664-676). If buf->size is smaller than buf->len + len, it sets size to 64 if it was 0 and doubles it until it is at least buf->len + len, then reallocates buf->s with xrealloc (667-673). It copies len characters from s to buf->s+buf->len with memcpy and increases buf->len by len (674-675). The caller must supply len readable characters in s, and no overflow check is made on buf->len + len or on the size doubling. No NUL is added.
note: [R:n/a] fixed-unreviewed in the packet; checked against tc.str.c:664-676 (the old prose said no overflow, which the code does not check; stated as a caller requirement).

name: STRBUF##_append(struct STRBUF *buf, const CHAR *s)
prose: Generated functions strbuf_append and Strbuf_append (tc.str.c:678-682): each calls STRBUF##_appendn(buf, s, STRLEN(s)) with STRLEN being strlen for strbuf and Strlen for Strbuf, so it appends the characters of the NUL-terminated string s, without the terminating NUL, and grows the buffer as appendn does.
note: [R:n/a] fixed-unreviewed in the packet; checked against tc.str.c:678-682 and 709-710.

name: STRBUF##_finish(struct STRBUF *buf)
prose: Generated functions strbuf_finish and Strbuf_finish (tc.str.c:684-689): they append a NUL with STRBUF##_append1(buf, 0), which increments buf->len so that it counts the NUL, and return xrealloc(buf->s, buf->len * sizeof(*buf->s)), the buffer shrunk or grown to exactly len entries. buf->s is not updated with the returned pointer, so if xrealloc moved the block buf->s is left pointing to the old block; the buffer is meant to be handed to the caller and the Strbuf not used again.
note: [R:n/a] fixed-unreviewed in the packet; checked against tc.str.c:684-689 (append1 at 657-662).

name: STRBUF##_cleanup(void *xbuf)
prose: Generated functions strbuf_cleanup and Strbuf_cleanup (tc.str.c:691-698): they treat xbuf as a struct strbuf (or Strbuf) pointer and call xfree(buf->s); the struct is not freed, buf->s is not set to NULL, and len and size are not changed.
note: [R:n/a] fixed-unreviewed in the packet; checked against tc.str.c:691-698 (xfree not read, so whether xfree accepts NULL is not stated).

name: STRBUF##_free(void *xbuf)
prose: Generated functions strbuf_free and Strbuf_free (tc.str.c:700-705): they call STRBUF##_cleanup(xbuf), which frees buf->s, and then xfree(xbuf), which frees the struct itself; afterwards both the struct and its s pointer are dangling.
note: [R:n/a] fixed-unreviewed in the packet; checked against tc.str.c:700-705.
